For a system $s$ of constitution $c$, the process model fixes one Galilean inertial chart $g_s$ for kinetic-energy bookkeeping and transfer records and holds that chart fixed throughout each process. A process record is a tuple
$$P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P).$$
For each finite closed time interval $I_P=[t_0,t_1]\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $t_0<t_1$ as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, its component fields have these types: $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$ are equilibrium endpoint coordinates from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; $Z_s$ is the model-declared configuration space of the system, its auxiliaries and devices; $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq Z_s$ is the model-declared set of equilibrium configurations and $\xi_s:Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\to D_c$ assigns their state coordinates; $z_P:I_P\to Z_s$ is a function ([[def-function]]); $\mathcal K_s$ is the model-declared set of control/contact records and $\kappa_P\in\mathcal K_s$; and $\mathcal R_s$ is the model-declared set of signed transfer records and $r_P\in\mathcal R_s$. These fields form a finite Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]]). The admitted records $\mathcal P_s$ are the model-specified subset of tuples with these types that additionally satisfy $z_P(t_0),z_P(t_1)\in Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\xi_s(z_P(t_0))=x_P^-$, and $\xi_s(z_P(t_1))=x_P^+$. No continuity or differentiability is imposed on $z_P$, and its values at interior times need not represent equilibrium states.

For an endpoint bookkeeping quantity $F$, write $\Delta F=F_P^+-F_P^-$. A closed record in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]] has no matter crossing the chosen outer boundary throughout $I_P$; zero net matter transfer alone does not suffice. The core closed-record class $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\subseteq\mathcal P_s$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) consists exactly of the closed records $P\in\mathcal P_s$ for which the system has a supplied fixed total mass $M>0$ and defined center-of-mass velocities at both endpoints in the fixed chart $g_s$, and $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$. Here $K_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm\|_2^2$ are defined as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U_{\mathrm{ext}}^\pm$ are supplied endpoint values of any model-specified external-field potential energy tracked separately from the internal-energy coordinate in $g_s$; if no such term is tracked, both values are set to zero. Other process classes require an expanded energy bookkeeping rule.

Heat is the protocol-assigned thermal mode of energy transfer across the selected outer boundary, not a quantity stored in the equilibrium state. For each admitted $P$, its transfer record $r_P$ supplies cumulative incoming and outgoing thermal energies $H_P^{\mathrm{in}},H_P^{\mathrm{out}}:I_P\to[0,\infty)$, with numerical values in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. Both maps start at zero at $t_0$ and satisfy $H_P^a(t)\le H_P^a(u)$ whenever $t\le u$ in $I_P$, for $a\in\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{out}\}$. Their increments record the total thermal energy transferred in each direction over the corresponding time interval, across all declared outer-boundary thermal channels, before cancellation between directions or channels. No continuity or differentiability of these maps is required. Transfers between subsystems inside that boundary are internal and are excluded from these outer-boundary totals.

Define $Q:\mathcal P_s\to\mathbb R$ by $Q[P]:=H_P^{\mathrm{in}}(t_1)-H_P^{\mathrm{out}}(t_1)$. The protocol also supplies $W_{\mathrm{on}}:\mathcal P_s\to\mathbb R$, with values in joules; both transfers use the fixed bookkeeping chart $g_s$. Thus $Q[P]>0$ means net thermal energy enters the system, and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$ means net mechanical work is done on it. These are functionals of the process record, not state functions of $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$. A record $P\in\mathcal P_s$ is adiabatic exactly when $H_P^{\mathrm{in}}(t)=H_P^{\mathrm{out}}(t)=0$ for every $t\in I_P$: no thermal energy crosses the selected boundary throughout the record. In particular an adiabatic record has $Q[P]=0$, but zero net heat alone does not specify an adiabatic record. On $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$, use the restrictions of these same maps; defining them on the larger class supplies no energy-balance law for records outside the core class. A closed record may still exchange energy; it is not thereby isolated.

A preparation is a model-specified rule selecting the particular initial equilibrium state $x_P^-$. A statistical extension may instead specify a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space, as in [[def-probability-measure]]; such a statistical preparation is outside this deterministic process class. A preparation does not assert later equilibration. An admitted record may pass through nonequilibrium configurations even though both endpoints lie in $D_c$.

For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, no thermal energy crosses its selected outer boundary throughout the record, so $H_P^{\mathrm{in}}(t)=H_P^{\mathrm{out}}(t)=0$ for every $t\in I_P$ and hence $Q[P]=0$; the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound. Fix the finite constituent split $s_1,\ldots,s_m$ used for the endpoint bookkeeping, with $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, and constitutions $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. Every additional named auxiliary or work device has an endpoint set $Y_j$, energy map, and adopted entropy map $S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}$ as in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. Every constituent whose entropy can change must occur either in the thermodynamic split or through one of these explicit auxiliary maps. Every auxiliary is retained in the complete endpoint tuples and energy constraints. An explicitly entropy-neutral device may be assigned $S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}=0$; more generally an auxiliary with declared zero endpoint entropy change cancels in the displayed inequality, while its variable state and energy remain in $\mathcal F$. Its endpoint product is

$$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}:=(D_{c_1}\times\cdots\times D_{c_m})\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_k,\qquad \mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}},$$

where $\mathcal F$ is the model-declared feasible endpoint set for the fixed totals, retained barriers, and permitted exchanges, as in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The process model supplies an endpoint association on the two formal endpoint labels $-$ and $+$:

$$\rho_P:\{-,+\}\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad \rho_P(-)=\mathbf x_P^-=(x_{1,P}^-,\ldots,x_{m,P}^-,y_{1,P}^-,\ldots,y_{k,P}^-),\qquad \rho_P(+)=\mathbf x_P^+=(x_{1,P}^+,\ldots,x_{m,P}^+,y_{1,P}^+,\ldots,y_{k,P}^+),$$

where $\mathbf x_P^-$ and $\mathbf x_P^+$ are respectively the declared constituent-state tuples including all auxiliary endpoint states and representing the aggregate equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$ of $P$. Both tuples must belong to the same $\mathcal F$. Restrict to endpoint splits admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] as a collection of independent separated macroscopic systems, so that its additive entropy rule applies to the macroscopic split; additionally adopt additivity of the explicitly modeled auxiliary entropy contributions for the complete compound. For $k=0$ this is the original thermodynamic-only split. On this admitted $\mathcal F$, define

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}(y_j)\qquad\left(\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_k)\in\mathcal F\right).$$

This uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]].

The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))\ge0.$$

The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))=0$. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound with the chosen independent separated macroscopic subsystem split and any explicitly modeled named auxiliaries, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x),\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}(y_j),$$

Here $\max$ means that $x^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathcal F$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})\ge S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal F$, using maximum in the sense of [[def-max-min]]. Here $x=(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a complete endpoint tuple from [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]; $k=0$ gives the original thermodynamic-only formula. The finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. The macroscopic summands are those of the separated constituents under [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], and any auxiliary summands are the explicitly adopted endpoint entropy maps of the same complete compound model. This route assumes that these contributions add for the complete admitted split. A constant auxiliary entropy may be dropped as an additive constant when comparing maxima, whereas variable auxiliary entropy must be retained. Whenever the stable-equilibrium label is used, attainment is assumed: at least one maximizing endpoint lies in $\mathcal F$. If $\mathcal F$ is empty or the entropy supremum is not attained, this item supplies no equilibrium state.

“Global” refers to every endpoint in this exact $\mathcal F$, not just nearby states, states reachable by a restricted short-time dynamics, or states on a selected branch. A local maximum that is not global, or a long-lived preparation trapped by kinetic barriers, is not declared stable equilibrium by this postulate. No uniqueness or relaxation dynamics is assumed.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: By [A2] and [F2], $\Delta U_c[P_s]=Q[P_s]-p_0\Delta V_c[P_s]$. By [A1]–[A3], the total entropy change along the isolated-compound extension is $\Delta S_{\rm tot}[\widehat P]=\Delta S_c[P_s]-Q[P_s]/T_0$, because the pressure store has constant entropy. Therefore $$ \Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)=\Delta U_c[P_s]+p_0\Delta V_c[P_s]-T_0\Delta S_c[P_s]=Q[P_s]-T_0\Delta S_c[P_s]=-T_0\Delta S_{\rm tot}[\widehat P]\le0 $$ by $T_0>0$ and [F3]. The heat and work are assigned to $P_s$, while their matching reservoir and store changes are assigned to its same-record extension $\widehat P$.

For every $(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F$, [A2]–[A3] give $E_R(y_R)=E_{\rm tot}-U_c(x)-p_0V_c(x)-C_B$. By [A1], reservoir entropy is affine in this energy, while the pressure-store entropy is constant. Additivity of the constituent entropies therefore gives one constant $C_0$, independent of the feasible tuple, such that $$ S_{\rm tot}(x,y_R,y_B)=C_0-\frac{\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x)}{T_0}. $$ Since $T_0>0$, an attained global maximizer on $\mathcal F$ has a system component that minimizes $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on every $x$ in the projection $\Pi_s(\mathcal F)$. This proves the global-minimum conclusion on the precise induced feasible set.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Fix a closed system $s$ of constitution $c$, with equilibrium domain $D_c$ from *Equilibrium state domains*, and fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$. Define, for $x\in D_c$,
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U_c(x)+p_0V_c(x)-T_0S_c(x),
$$
where $U_c,V_c$ are the dimensioned energy and volume maps of *Equilibrium state domains* and $S_c$ is the adopted entropy of *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*. Thus $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ has units joules.

Let $P_s\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ be an admitted closed system process record as defined in *Thermodynamic process records and transfer conventions*, with system endpoints $x_{P_s}^-,x_{P_s}^+\in D_c$. Let $R$ be its ideal thermal reservoir and $B$ its ideal pressure store; both lie inside a declared isolated-compound outer boundary. Let $\widehat P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s\sqcup R\sqcup B)$ be an admitted core closed process record for that isolated compound, whose supplied total mass is positive, whose endpoint center-of-mass velocities are defined in one fixed Galilean chart, and whose compound center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change. These are conditions on the whole compound, additional to the system-record conditions. By an extension, require that $\widehat P$ has the same time interval, system endpoints, system configuration path, and system-side protocol and transfer records as $P_s$, together with the reservoir and store records. Write its compound endpoint association as
$$
\rho_{\widehat P}(\pm)=(x_{P_s}^\pm,y_R^\pm,y_B^\pm)\in\mathcal F\subseteq D_c\times Y_R\times Y_B,
$$
where $Y_R,Y_B$ are the model-declared reservoir and store equilibrium state sets, represented as admitted constituent state domains (or subsets thereof) in the second-law endpoint split; $E_R,E_B$ and their entropies are the corresponding dimensioned state maps. The split is admitted as independent separated macroscopic systems by *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*. The set $\mathcal F$ is the exact feasible endpoint set from *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The system protocol assigns heat $Q[P_s]$ and work $W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ to $P_s$; the auxiliary endpoint changes in $\widehat P$ satisfy the reservoir and store relations in [A1]–[A2] below. No matter crosses the compound boundary, no work channel other than pressure-store work acts on the system, and no other energy-coordinate changes are omitted.

Then the system endpoint difference obeys
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)\le0.
$$
If the final compound endpoint $\rho_{\widehat P}(+)$ is an attained global entropy maximum on $\mathcal F$, then $x_{P_s}^+$ attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on the system projection
$$
\Pi_s(\mathcal F):=\{x\in D_c:\exists y_R\in Y_R,\ y_B\in Y_B\text{ with }(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F\}.
$$
This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

Fix a closed system $s$ of constitution $c$, with equilibrium domain $D_c$ from *Equilibrium state domains*, and fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$. Define, for $x\in D_c$,
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U_c(x)+p_0V_c(x)-T_0S_c(x),
$$
where $U_c,V_c$ are the dimensioned energy and volume maps of *Equilibrium state domains* and $S_c$ is the adopted entropy of *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*. Thus $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ has units joules.

Let $P_s\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ be an admitted closed system process record as defined in *Thermodynamic process records and transfer conventions*, with system endpoints $x_{P_s}^-,x_{P_s}^+\in D_c$. Let $R$ be its ideal thermal reservoir and $B$ its ideal pressure store; both lie inside a declared isolated-compound outer boundary. Let $\widehat P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s\sqcup R\sqcup B)$ be an admitted core closed process record for that isolated compound, whose supplied total mass is positive, whose endpoint center-of-mass velocities are defined in one fixed Galilean chart, and whose compound center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change. These are conditions on the whole compound, additional to the system-record conditions. By an extension, require that $\widehat P$ has the same time interval, system endpoints, system configuration path, and system-side protocol and transfer records as $P_s$, together with the reservoir and store records. Write its compound endpoint association as
$$
\rho_{\widehat P}(\pm)=(x_{P_s}^\pm,y_R^\pm,y_B^\pm)\in\mathcal F\subseteq D_c\times Y_R\times Y_B,
$$
where $Y_R,Y_B$ are the model-declared reservoir and store equilibrium state sets, represented as admitted constituent state domains (or subsets thereof) in the second-law endpoint split; $E_R,E_B$ and their entropies are the corresponding dimensioned state maps. The split is admitted as independent separated macroscopic systems by *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*. The set $\mathcal F$ is the exact feasible endpoint set from *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The system protocol assigns heat $Q[P_s]$ and work $W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ to $P_s$; the auxiliary endpoint changes in $\widehat P$ satisfy the reservoir and store relations in [A1]–[A2] below. No matter crosses the compound boundary, no work channel other than pressure-store work acts on the system, and no other energy-coordinate changes are omitted.

Then the system endpoint difference obeys
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)\le0.
$$
If the final compound endpoint $\rho_{\widehat P}(+)$ is an attained global entropy maximum on $\mathcal F$, then $x_{P_s}^+$ attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on the system projection
$$
\Pi_s(\mathcal F):=\{x\in D_c:\exists y_R\in Y_R,\ y_B\in Y_B\text{ with }(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F\}.
$$
This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For a system $s$ of constitution $c$, the process model fixes one Galilean inertial chart $g_s$ for kinetic-energy bookkeeping and transfer records and holds that chart fixed throughout each process. A process record is a tuple
$$P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P).$$
For each finite closed time interval $I_P=[t_0,t_1]\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $t_0<t_1$ as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, its component fields have these types: $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$ are equilibrium endpoint coordinates from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; $Z_s$ is the model-declared configuration space of the system, its auxiliaries and devices; $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq Z_s$ is the model-declared set of equilibrium configurations and $\xi_s:Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\to D_c$ assigns their state coordinates; $z_P:I_P\to Z_s$ is a function ([[def-function]]); $\mathcal K_s$ is the model-declared set of control/contact records and $\kappa_P\in\mathcal K_s$; and $\mathcal R_s$ is the model-declared set of signed transfer records and $r_P\in\mathcal R_s$. These fields form a finite Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]]). The admitted records $\mathcal P_s$ are the model-specified subset of tuples with these types that additionally satisfy $z_P(t_0),z_P(t_1)\in Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\xi_s(z_P(t_0))=x_P^-$, and $\xi_s(z_P(t_1))=x_P^+$. No continuity or differentiability is imposed on $z_P$, and its values at interior times need not represent equilibrium states.

For an endpoint bookkeeping quantity $F$, write $\Delta F=F_P^+-F_P^-$. A closed record in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]] has no matter crossing the chosen outer boundary throughout $I_P$; zero net matter transfer alone does not suffice. The core closed-record class $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\subseteq\mathcal P_s$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) consists exactly of the closed records $P\in\mathcal P_s$ for which the system has a supplied fixed total mass $M>0$ and defined center-of-mass velocities at both endpoints in the fixed chart $g_s$, and $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$. Here $K_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm\|_2^2$ are defined as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U_{\mathrm{ext}}^\pm$ are supplied endpoint values of any model-specified external-field potential energy tracked separately from the internal-energy coordinate in $g_s$; if no such term is tracked, both values are set to zero. Other process classes require an expanded energy bookkeeping rule.

Heat is the protocol-assigned thermal mode of energy transfer across the selected outer boundary, not a quantity stored in the equilibrium state. For each admitted $P$, its transfer record $r_P$ supplies cumulative incoming and outgoing thermal energies $H_P^{\mathrm{in}},H_P^{\mathrm{out}}:I_P\to[0,\infty)$, with numerical values in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. Both maps start at zero at $t_0$ and satisfy $H_P^a(t)\le H_P^a(u)$ whenever $t\le u$ in $I_P$, for $a\in\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{out}\}$. Their increments record the total thermal energy transferred in each direction over the corresponding time interval, across all declared outer-boundary thermal channels, before cancellation between directions or channels. No continuity or differentiability of these maps is required. Transfers between subsystems inside that boundary are internal and are excluded from these outer-boundary totals.

Define $Q:\mathcal P_s\to\mathbb R$ by $Q[P]:=H_P^{\mathrm{in}}(t_1)-H_P^{\mathrm{out}}(t_1)$. The protocol also supplies $W_{\mathrm{on}}:\mathcal P_s\to\mathbb R$, with values in joules; both transfers use the fixed bookkeeping chart $g_s$. Thus $Q[P]>0$ means net thermal energy enters the system, and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$ means net mechanical work is done on it. These are functionals of the process record, not state functions of $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$. A record $P\in\mathcal P_s$ is adiabatic exactly when $H_P^{\mathrm{in}}(t)=H_P^{\mathrm{out}}(t)=0$ for every $t\in I_P$: no thermal energy crosses the selected boundary throughout the record. In particular an adiabatic record has $Q[P]=0$, but zero net heat alone does not specify an adiabatic record. On $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$, use the restrictions of these same maps; defining them on the larger class supplies no energy-balance law for records outside the core class. A closed record may still exchange energy; it is not thereby isolated.

A preparation is a model-specified rule selecting the particular initial equilibrium state $x_P^-$. A statistical extension may instead specify a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space, as in [[def-probability-measure]]; such a statistical preparation is outside this deterministic process class. A preparation does not assert later equilibration. An admitted record may pass through nonequilibrium configurations even though both endpoints lie in $D_c$.

The isolated-compound record $\widehat P$ records the auxiliary endpoint states and extension of that system record.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound. Fix the finite constituent split $s_1,\ldots,s_m$ used for the endpoint bookkeeping, with $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, and constitutions $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. Every additional named auxiliary or work device has an endpoint set $Y_j$, energy map, and adopted entropy map $S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}$ as in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. Every constituent whose entropy can change must occur either in the thermodynamic split or through one of these explicit auxiliary maps. Every auxiliary is retained in the complete endpoint tuples and energy constraints. An explicitly entropy-neutral device may be assigned $S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}=0$; more generally an auxiliary with declared zero endpoint entropy change cancels in the displayed inequality, while its variable state and energy remain in $\mathcal F$. Its endpoint product is

$$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}:=(D_{c_1}\times\cdots\times D_{c_m})\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_k,\qquad \mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}},$$

where $\mathcal F$ is the model-declared feasible endpoint set for the fixed totals, retained barriers, and permitted exchanges, as in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The process model supplies an endpoint association on the two formal endpoint labels $-$ and $+$:

$$\rho_P:\{-,+\}\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad \rho_P(-)=\mathbf x_P^-=(x_{1,P}^-,\ldots,x_{m,P}^-,y_{1,P}^-,\ldots,y_{k,P}^-),\qquad \rho_P(+)=\mathbf x_P^+=(x_{1,P}^+,\ldots,x_{m,P}^+,y_{1,P}^+,\ldots,y_{k,P}^+),$$

where $\mathbf x_P^-$ and $\mathbf x_P^+$ are respectively the declared constituent-state tuples including all auxiliary endpoint states and representing the aggregate equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$ of $P$. Both tuples must belong to the same $\mathcal F$. Restrict to endpoint splits admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] as a collection of independent separated macroscopic systems, so that its additive entropy rule applies to the macroscopic split; additionally adopt additivity of the explicitly modeled auxiliary entropy contributions for the complete compound. For $k=0$ this is the original thermodynamic-only split. On this admitted $\mathcal F$, define

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}(y_j)\qquad\left(\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_k)\in\mathcal F\right).$$

This uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]].

The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))\ge0.$$

The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))=0$. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials* give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of *Finite sums and finite products, by recursion*. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling*. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in *Thermodynamic response functions on valid local charts* and *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* and *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*, on the exact feasible set of *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in *Stable equilibrium requires an attained global entropy maximum*. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. The nonnegative integral defined by
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] equals the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral
defined by [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]], with the same value in
$[0,+\infty]$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

derivations.claim: The map $h$ is continuous, so [L2] makes $H$ compact. For every Borel probability $P$ on $K$, each coordinate of $h$ is bounded and Borel. Compactness and [L1] give boundedness. If $|f|\le M$ for one such coordinate, [F3] gives $\int_K|f|\,dP\le M P(K)=M$, so $f$ is integrable.

Every point of $C$ is a finite convex combination of points $h(x_i)$. If such a representation has $N>d+2$, the linear map $T:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+2}$ defined by $T(c)=(\sum_i c_i h(x_i),\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector $c$ by [L3], because the coordinate bases give domain dimension $N$ and codomain dimension $d+2$. Thus $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i h(x_i)=0$, so $c$ has both positive and negative coordinates. After dropping zero weights from the representation, set $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace each weight $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. The new weights remain nonnegative, still sum to one, represent the same point, and at least one is zero. Repeating reduces every combination to at most $d+2$ terms. Hence $C$ is the image of $K^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$ under $\Theta((x_i),(\theta_i))=\sum_{i=1}^{d+2}\theta_i h(x_i)$, where $\Delta_{d+2}:=\{(\theta_i):\theta_i\ge0,\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; shorter combinations are padded with zero weights and any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Each factor $K$ is closed and bounded by [L2], and $\Delta_{d+2}$ is closed by continuity of the finite coordinate sum and its coordinate inequalities; it is bounded since $0\le\theta_i\le1$. Their product is therefore closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{(d+1)(d+2)}$, so compact by [L2]. To check $\Theta$ is continuous on this compact parameter set, fix a parameter $((x_i),(\theta_i))$. Each coordinate $h_j$ is bounded by some $M$ on $K$ and is continuous at each of the finitely many $x_i$. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose neighborhoods of the $x_i$ making $|h_j(x_i')-h_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/(2N)$ for every output coordinate $j$, and require $|\theta_i'-\theta_i|<\epsilon/(2N(M+1))$. Since $0\le\theta_i'\le1$ and $|h_j(x_i)|\le M$, each product difference $|\theta_i'h_j(x_i')-\theta_ih_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/N$; summing over $i$ makes each output-coordinate difference smaller than $\epsilon$. Thus $\Theta$ is continuous. The continuous-image clause of [L2] makes its image $C$ compact, and [L2] also makes $C$ closed.

Fix any Borel probability $P$ on $K$ and let $y(P):=(\int_K x\,dP,\int_Ks\,dP)=\int_Kh\,dP$, with coordinatewise integration. For $\epsilon>0$, compactness of $H$ gives a finite cover of $H$ by open Euclidean balls of radius $\epsilon$. Their preimages under $h$ are Borel; disjointifying them in a fixed finite order gives a finite Borel partition $(A_i)$ of $K$. For every nonempty part choose $z_i\in A_i$ and put $\theta_i=P(A_i)$. Then $y_\epsilon:=\sum_i\theta_i h(z_i)$ belongs to $C$. For $x\in A_i$, both $h(x)$ and $h(z_i)$ lie in the same radius-$\epsilon$ ball, so each coordinate difference is at most $2\epsilon$. The simple map equal to $h(z_i)$ on $A_i$ has integral $y_\epsilon$ by the simple-integral definition. By linearity and the integral triangle inequality in [F3], each coordinate of $y(P)-y_\epsilon$ has absolute value at most $2\epsilon\sum_iP(A_i)=2\epsilon$. Consequently $\|y(P)-y_\epsilon\|_2\le2\epsilon\sqrt{d+1}$, so the sequence obtained with $\epsilon=1/n$ converges to $y(P)$. Since $C$ is closed by step 2.1, $y(P)\in C$.

Because $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, a finite convex combination of generators has barycenter $\bar x$; its corresponding combination of points $h(x)$ shows that $E_{\bar x}:=\{r\in\mathbb R:(\bar x,r)\in C\}$ is nonempty. The set $E_{\bar x}$ is bounded because $C$ is bounded, and it is closed because $C$ is closed and $r\mapsto(\bar x,r)$ is continuous. By [L2] it is compact in $\mathbb R$, so [L1] applied to the identity function yields a maximum $r_*\in E_{\bar x}$.

Represent $(\bar x,r_*)\in C$ by a finite convex combination $\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i(x_i,s(x_i))$, dropping zero weights. If $N>d+1$, the linear map $R:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ given by $R(c)=(\sum_i c_ix_i,\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector by [L3], since its domain dimension is $N$ and its codomain dimension is $d+1$. Hence $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_ix_i=0$, with both signs among the $c_i$. If $\sum_i c_is(x_i)\ne0$, choose the sign of $c$ so that this sum is positive. For sufficiently small $t>0$, the weights $\theta_i+tc_i$ are nonnegative, preserve total mass and barycenter, and increase the last coordinate above $r_*$, contradicting maximality in step 3.2. Thus $\sum_i c_is(x_i)=0$. Now take $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. This removes at least one positive weight while preserving total mass, barycenter, and entropy value $r_*$. Repeating finitely many times leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights.

Let $P_*:=\sum_i\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ be the probability measure from step 4.1. Each $\delta_{x_i}$ is countably additive because among disjoint Borel sets at most one contains $x_i$, and $\delta_{x_i}(K)=1$; hence $P_*$ is a Borel probability measure. It has barycenter $\bar x$ and entropy $r_*$, so it is feasible by the model assumption. For any other feasible Borel probability $P$, step 3.1 gives $(\bar x,\int s\,dP)\in C$, so $\int s\,dP\le r_*$. Thus $P_*$ attains the entropy maximum among all Borel mixtures and has at most $d+1$ atoms. No finite generator menu was assumed.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless generator coordinates. Each $x\in K$ labels one model-specified phase-generator state; the model assigns it entropy per mole $s(x)\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $s:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, using the numerical entropy value in that fixed unit. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ to be the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$. A Borel probability mixture is a countably additive probability measure $P$ on that sigma algebra; its barycenter and entropy per mole are the coordinatewise integrals $\int_Kx\,dP$ and $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $x\in K$, define the unit point mass $\delta_x$ by $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise, for Borel $A\subseteq K$. Assume every Borel probability mixture with barycenter $\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. Then there are $m\le d+1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in K$, and weights $\theta_i\ge0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1$ such that $P_*:=\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a feasible Borel probability mixture and $\int_Ks\,dP_*\ge\int_Ks\,dP$ for every feasible mixture $P$.

Here integrals use the measure convention of *Measure space and integral*. The entropy map is part of the model; this theorem derives neither its microscopic meaning nor compactness of a physical phase domain.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials* give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of *Finite sums and finite products, by recursion*. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling*. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in *Thermodynamic response functions on valid local charts* and *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* and *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*, on the exact feasible set of *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in *Stable equilibrium requires an attained global entropy maximum*. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$
