citations.quote:
Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

Fix a material constitution $c$, with $r$ named species and dimensionless equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, define the diagonal SI coordinate map

$$\Phi_c(x):=(U_c(x),V_c(x),n_{c,1}(x),\ldots,n_{c,r}(x))=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\ldots,\hat n_r\,\mathrm{mol}).$$

In SI numerical coordinates this is a diagonal linear bijection with a diagonal linear inverse, so it maps ambient open sets to open sets and its inverse is defined on its image.

Choose an open subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the ambient dimensionless Euclidean coordinates that is designated as a single-phase chart, and set $\Omega:=\Phi_c(O)$, an open chart of physical SI coordinate values. Here $U$ is the internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. If $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ is the entropy adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], define its physical-coordinate representative on $\Omega$ by

$$S_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R.$$

When its arguments are the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, write this representative as $S_c(U,V,n)$ for brevity. On $\Omega$, assume the finite representative is $C^2$ and has $S_{c,U}>0$, as adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in the physical $U$ coordinate while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; in particular the conversion factor from $\hat U$ is included.

Explicitly, with the partial derivatives on the right taken in the dimensionless coordinates on $O$ while holding every other hatted coordinate fixed, the physical partials are

$$S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial_{\hat U}S_c,\qquad S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{m^3})^{-1}\partial_{\hat V}S_c,\qquad S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{mol})^{-1}\partial_{\hat n_j}S_c,$$

using the coordinate-conversion convention of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]].

Define the physical-coordinate representatives of the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

derivations.claim: From the displayed $g^\gamma$ and [A1], at the center $S_T=m_\gamma c/T_0$, $U_T=m_\gamma c$, $V_T=0$, and $V_p=-m_\gamma\kappa$, so the fixed-composition/amount $(T,p)$ Jacobian for $(U,V)$ is $-m_\gamma^2c\kappa$. The map $(x_1,x_2,m_\gamma)\mapsto(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ has determinant $m_\gamma^2(x_1+x_2+x_3)=m_\gamma^2$. Hence the full state-map Jacobian is $-m_\gamma^4c\kappa\ne0$, and [L2] gives the specified open full-state inverse patch, which can be shrunk to retain positive temperature, volume and amounts. On this patch, [L1] and the conjugate assignments give $dG=-S\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$ and $dU=T\,dS-p\,dV+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$, so $dS=T^{-1}dU+(p/T)dV-\sum_j(\mu_j/T)dn_j$. The inverse coordinates and chemical potentials are $C^1$; by [L3], all these coefficients are $C^1$. Thus the entropy representative is $C^2$ and has $S_U=1/T>0$, $S_V=p/T$, and $S_{n_j}=-\mu_j/T$, verifying the derivative-defined quantities of [F2].

For $m=n_1+n_2+n_3$ and $x_j=n_j/m$, [L1] at fixed $T,p$ and the other two species amounts gives
$$
\mu_1=g+(1-x_1)g_{x_1}-x_2g_{x_2},\quad \mu_2=g-x_1g_{x_1}+(1-x_2)g_{x_2},\quad \mu_3=g-x_1g_{x_1}-x_2g_{x_2}.
$$
Substitution of the two stated $g^\gamma$ at the centered point gives $\mu^\alpha=\mu^\beta=(0,0,0)$. Thus $F_i=\mu_i^\beta-\mu_i^\alpha=0$ and $A=\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu^\alpha=0$.

From the formulas in step 2.1, at the centered point
$$
D_{(x_1,x_2)}\mu^\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}2a_\gamma/3&-a_\gamma/3\\-a_\gamma/3&2a_\gamma/3\\-a_\gamma/3&-a_\gamma/3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \partial_p\mu^\gamma=(v_0,v_0,v_0+q_\gamma)^{\mathsf T}.
$$
Using $a_\beta=\eta$, $a_\alpha=2\eta$, $q_\beta=q$, and $q_\alpha=0$, the derivative minor of $(F_1,F_2,F_3,A)$ in columns $(x_1^\beta,x_2^\beta,p,x_1^\alpha)$ is
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 2\eta/3&-\eta/3&0&-4\eta/3\\ -\eta/3&2\eta/3&0&2\eta/3\\ -\eta/3&-\eta/3&q&2\eta/3\\ 0&0&-v_0/2&-5a_\alpha/6 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The cofactor of the last-row pressure entry is zero because, after deleting that row and column, the fourth column is $-2$ times the first. Expansion along the last row therefore gives determinant $(-5a_\alpha/6)q(\eta^2/3)\ne0$. The combined equation map therefore has the required rank four.

The ambient coordinate dimension is $d=2+P(C-1)=6$, and the number of equations is $q_{\rm eq}+R=C(P-1)+R=3+1=4$, where $q_{\rm eq}:=C(P-1)$ is a dimensionless equation count distinct from the volume-per-mole parameter $q$. By [F1], the local equation zero set has dimension $6-4=2$, agreeing with $C-P+2-R=3-2+2-1=2$. This is only the full-rank equation-set calculation.

Take $C=3$ species and $P=2$ phases. Write $x_3:=1-x_1-x_2$, and center the open composition charts at $x_1=x_2=x_3=1/3$. Fix $T_0>0$, $p_0>0$, $s_0,c,v_0,\kappa,q>0$, and $\eta=1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The parameters have units $s_0,c\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $v_0\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, $\kappa\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$, and $q\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. For $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, set $a_\alpha=2\eta$, $a_\beta=\eta$, $q_\alpha=0$, and $q_\beta=q$, and define molar Gibbs potentials
$$
g^\gamma(T,p,x)=-s_0(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_0(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2+\frac{a_\gamma}{2}(x_1^2+x_2^2)-\frac{a_\gamma}{3}(x_1+x_2)+\frac{a_\gamma}{9}+q_\gamma(p-p_0)x_3.
$$
Set $G^\gamma=m_\gamma g^\gamma$ on each fixed-tag branch and adopt the natural Gibbs assignments $S=-G_T$, $V=G_p$, and $\mu_j=G_{n_j}$, with $U=G+TS-pV$. These smooth charts are scale-invariant in amount. Near the centered point the volumes are positive, and the $(U,V)$ chart Jacobian at fixed composition and amount is nonsingular: $U_T=m_\gamma c$, $V_p=-m_\gamma\kappa$, and $V_T=0$ there, so its determinant is $-m_\gamma^2c\kappa\ne0$. The reaction vector is $\nu=(-1,-1/2,1)^{\mathsf T}$, of rank $R=1$. At $(T_0,p_0,x_1,x_2)=(T_0,p_0,1/3,1/3)$, both phases have $\mu^\gamma=(0,0,0)$, so the phase-equality equations and reaction affinity vanish.

For each branch, fix a reference amount $m_*>0$ in moles. Choose an open neighborhood $\mathcal O$ of $(T_0,p_0,1/3,1/3,m_*)$ in $(0,\infty)^2\times\{(x_1,x_2):x_1,x_2>0,\ x_1+x_2<1\}\times(0,\infty)$, using $n=(mx_1,mx_2,m(1-x_1-x_2))$. Shrink this neighborhood to the inverse-function patch verified below; all component amounts remain positive. The constructed branch's local physical state map is $\chi:(T,p,x_1,x_2,m)\mapsto(U,V,mx_1,mx_2,m(1-x_1-x_2))$, on the positive amount and interior composition domain just specified. On the inverse patch verified below, define its numerical domain $O_c=\Phi_c^{-1}(\chi(\mathcal O))$ and declare this patch to be the local model's $D_c$ patch, where $\Phi_c(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\hat n_2,\hat n_3)=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\hat n_2\,\mathrm{mol},\hat n_3\,\mathrm{mol})$ is the unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Define the numerical entropy by $S_c=S^{\rm SI}\circ\Phi_c$, with $S^{\rm SI}$ supplied by the Gibbs assignments through this inverse. Thus the displayed derivatives are derivatives in physical SI coordinates on $\Phi_c(O_c)$; the model patch is not an empirical claim about an independently specified material domain.

Take $C=3$ species and $P=2$ phases. Write $x_3:=1-x_1-x_2$, and center the open composition charts at $x_1=x_2=x_3=1/3$. Fix $T_0>0$, $p_0>0$, $s_0,c,v_0,\kappa,q>0$, and $\eta=1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The parameters have units $s_0,c\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $v_0\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, $\kappa\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$, and $q\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. For $\gamma\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, set $a_\alpha=2\eta$, $a_\beta=\eta$, $q_\alpha=0$, and $q_\beta=q$, and define molar Gibbs potentials
$$
g^\gamma(T,p,x)=-s_0(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_0(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2+\frac{a_\gamma}{2}(x_1^2+x_2^2)-\frac{a_\gamma}{3}(x_1+x_2)+\frac{a_\gamma}{9}+q_\gamma(p-p_0)x_3.
$$
Set $G^\gamma=m_\gamma g^\gamma$ on each fixed-tag branch and adopt the natural Gibbs assignments $S=-G_T$, $V=G_p$, and $\mu_j=G_{n_j}$, with $U=G+TS-pV$. These smooth charts are scale-invariant in amount. Near the centered point the volumes are positive, and the $(U,V)$ chart Jacobian at fixed composition and amount is nonsingular: $U_T=m_\gamma c$, $V_p=-m_\gamma\kappa$, and $V_T=0$ there, so its determinant is $-m_\gamma^2c\kappa\ne0$. The reaction vector is $\nu=(-1,-1/2,1)^{\mathsf T}$, of rank $R=1$. At $(T_0,p_0,x_1,x_2)=(T_0,p_0,1/3,1/3)$, both phases have $\mu^\gamma=(0,0,0)$, so the phase-equality equations and reaction affinity vanish.

For each branch, fix a reference amount $m_*>0$ in moles. Choose an open neighborhood $\mathcal O$ of $(T_0,p_0,1/3,1/3,m_*)$ in $(0,\infty)^2\times\{(x_1,x_2):x_1,x_2>0,\ x_1+x_2<1\}\times(0,\infty)$, using $n=(mx_1,mx_2,m(1-x_1-x_2))$. Shrink this neighborhood to the inverse-function patch verified below; all component amounts remain positive. The constructed branch's local physical state map is $\chi:(T,p,x_1,x_2,m)\mapsto(U,V,mx_1,mx_2,m(1-x_1-x_2))$, on the positive amount and interior composition domain just specified. On the inverse patch verified below, define its numerical domain $O_c=\Phi_c^{-1}(\chi(\mathcal O))$ and declare this patch to be the local model's $D_c$ patch, where $\Phi_c(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\hat n_2,\hat n_3)=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\hat n_2\,\mathrm{mol},\hat n_3\,\mathrm{mol})$ is the unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Define the numerical entropy by $S_c=S^{\rm SI}\circ\Phi_c$, with $S^{\rm SI}$ supplied by the Gibbs assignments through this inverse. Thus the displayed derivatives are derivatives in physical SI coordinates on $\Phi_c(O_c)$; the model patch is not an empirical claim about an independently specified material domain.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$, with $r$ named species and dimensionless equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, define the diagonal SI coordinate map

$$\Phi_c(x):=(U_c(x),V_c(x),n_{c,1}(x),\ldots,n_{c,r}(x))=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\ldots,\hat n_r\,\mathrm{mol}).$$

In SI numerical coordinates this is a diagonal linear bijection with a diagonal linear inverse, so it maps ambient open sets to open sets and its inverse is defined on its image.

Choose an open subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the ambient dimensionless Euclidean coordinates that is designated as a single-phase chart, and set $\Omega:=\Phi_c(O)$, an open chart of physical SI coordinate values. Here $U$ is the internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. If $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ is the entropy adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], define its physical-coordinate representative on $\Omega$ by

$$S_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R.$$

When its arguments are the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, write this representative as $S_c(U,V,n)$ for brevity. On $\Omega$, assume the finite representative is $C^2$ and has $S_{c,U}>0$, as adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in the physical $U$ coordinate while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; in particular the conversion factor from $\hat U$ is included.

Explicitly, with the partial derivatives on the right taken in the dimensionless coordinates on $O$ while holding every other hatted coordinate fixed, the physical partials are

$$S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial_{\hat U}S_c,\qquad S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{m^3})^{-1}\partial_{\hat V}S_c,\qquad S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{mol})^{-1}\partial_{\hat n_j}S_c,$$

using the coordinate-conversion convention of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]].

Define the physical-coordinate representatives of the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

citations.quote:
Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. Suppose $V\subseteq\mathbb R^s$ is open, $n_*:=n^0+\nu\xi_*\in V$, $\Phi:V\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at $n_*$, and $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$ near $\xi_*$. For each $j$, let $e_j\in\mathbb R^s$ have coordinate $1$ in position $j$ and $0$ in every other position; define $\mu_j:=D\Phi(n_*)e_j$. Then

$$Df(\xi_*)h=\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h.$$

The tangent-cone and optimality claims are mathematical deductions. They do not assert that a particular physical system obeys this model or is at equilibrium.

derivations.claim:

u h)_A=-h\ge0$, or $h\le0$. The derivative data give $
u^{\mathsf T}\mu=-\mu_A+\mu_B=-1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, so $D\Phi(0)[h]=(
u^{\mathsf T}\mu)h\ge0$ for every feasible tangent extent. The units are joules because $h$ is in moles.

Directly, $\Phi(\xi)-\Phi(0)=-(1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}})\xi\ge0$ for every feasible $\xi\in[-1,0]$ mol, so the boundary point is a global minimum on this interval. The tangent-cone inequality is satisfied even though the interior equality $\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu=0$ fails.

Along $n(\xi)=(-\xi,1\,\mathrm{mol}+\xi)$, set $\Phi(\xi):=\widehat\Phi(n(\xi))=\Phi_0-(1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}})\xi$. Its derivative-defined amount coefficients are $\mu_A:=\partial_{n_A}\widehat\Phi=0$ and $\mu_B:=\partial_{n_B}\widehat\Phi=-1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, including at $\xi_*=0$ mol. This ambient extension is constructed optimization data only; no positive-mole thermodynamic chart at $n_A=0$ or physical realization is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix $C\ge1$ species and $R\ge1$ declared internal reaction extents. Let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{C\times R}$ be the dimensionless stoichiometric matrix, let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^C$ have units mol, and let $\xi\in\mathbb R^R$ have units mol. The amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$, and the nonnegative-amount feasible extent set is
$$
\mathcal F_\nu:=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^R:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^C\}.
$$
Assume the exact local reaction-feasible extent set is $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$; no additional local constraint removes any direction in its tangent cone.
Fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$ in a declared natural-variable chart. On an open neighborhood $U$ of a candidate endpoint $\xi_*$, let $\Phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be a finite $C^1$ constrained Gibbs-potential extension, in joules, satisfying
$$
D\Phi(\xi)[h]=\sum_{j=1}^C\mu_j(\xi)(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi))\cdot h,
$$
where every $\mu_j$ is in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. At positive amounts, require $\Phi(\xi)=U_c(x(\xi))+p_0V_c(x(\xi))-T_0S_c(x(\xi))$ for the system state $x(\xi)$, with $U_c,V_c,S_c$ from *Equilibrium state domains* and *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*; its derivative is that of the local Gibbs chart supplied by *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* and *Differentials of the thermodynamic potentials*.

If all amounts at $\xi_*$ are positive, assume $\xi_*$ is the system endpoint of a closed system process record and its admitted isolated-compound extension exactly as in *Fixed-temperature and fixed-pressure potential minimum with internal reactions*, is a global entropy-maximizing endpoint on that extension's exact feasible set, and the record's system projection contains every state $x(\xi)$ for $\xi\in\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. If at least one amount is zero, it is outside *Equilibrium state domains*; in that boundary case, assume instead that the model supplies a boundary-inclusive state domain with finite $C^1$ maps $\bar U_c,\bar V_c,\bar S_c:U\to\mathbb R$ in joules, $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, respectively, that $\Phi(\xi)=\bar U_c(\xi)+p_0\bar V_c(\xi)-T_0\bar S_c(\xi)$, and that its exact isolated-compound model has fixed total energy, an ideal reservoir with $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$, a constant-entropy pressure store satisfying $E_B-p_0\bar V_c(\xi)=C_B$, and a feasible-set projection equal to $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. Assume $\xi_*$ is an attained global entropy maximum on that boundary-inclusive set. This additional boundary model premise is not supplied by the positive-mole state chart or by *Fixed-temperature and fixed-pressure potential minimum with internal reactions*.

Under the relevant interior or boundary assumptions above, $\xi_*$ locally minimizes $\Phi$ on $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. Let $J_*:=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Then the first-order necessary condition is
$$
(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*))\cdot h\ge0\qquad\text{for every }h\in T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*),
$$
where
$$
T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*):=\{h\in\mathbb R^R:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J_*\}.
$$
If $\xi_*$ is interior to $\mathcal F_\nu$, this reduces to $\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*)=0$. If, in addition, $\Phi$ is convex and differentiable on a convex neighborhood containing the relevant feasible set, the same tangent inequality is sufficient for global minimization there.

historical_source_interface.exact_statement:
Fix $C\ge1$ species and $R\ge1$ declared internal reaction extents. Let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{C\times R}$ be the dimensionless stoichiometric matrix, let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^C$ have units mol, and let $\xi\in\mathbb R^R$ have units mol. The amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$, and the nonnegative-amount feasible extent set is
\[
\mathcal F_\nu:=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^R:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^C\}.
\]
Fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0$ in a declared natural-variable chart. Let $\Phi(\xi)$ be the constrained Gibbs potential on an open neighborhood $U$ of an equilibrium extent $\xi_*$, and assume the model supplies a finite $C^1$ extension through every zero-amount boundary point under consideration. On $U$, assume
\[
D\Phi(\xi)[h]=\sum_{j=1}^C\mu_j(\xi)(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi))\cdot h,
\]
where $\mu_j$ are the molar chemical potentials in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. This extension and derivative identity are not supplied by the positive-mole phase chart itself.

Suppose $\xi_*$ is an attained stable equilibrium for the fixed-$T_0,p_0$ internal reaction model with the ideal reservoirs of [[pthm-td-fixed-tp-reaction-potential-minimum]]. Then $\xi_*$ minimizes $\Phi$ on the exact reaction-feasible set locally. Let $J_*:=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. The feasible tangent cone is
\[
T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*):=\{h\in\mathbb R^R:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J_*\}.
\]
The first-order necessary condition is
\[
(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*))\cdot h\ge0\qquad(h\in T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*)).
\]
If $\xi_*$ is interior to $\mathcal F_\nu$, this reduces to $\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*)=0$. If, in addition, $\Phi$ is convex and differentiable on a convex neighborhood containing the relevant feasible set, the same tangent inequality is sufficient for global minimization there.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$. A countable probability law on $I$ means a nonnegative family with total sum $1$ under the finite-subsum convention above; these weights form such a law because $\sum_i p_i(\beta)=Z(\beta)/Z(\beta)=1$. For any real family $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open ([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]). A function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic on $U$** if, for every $c\in U$, there are a real $r>0$ and real coefficients $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that $N_r(c)\subseteq U$ and

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n\qquad(x\in N_r(c)).$$

The representing series must converge throughout this neighbourhood ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]], [[def-neighbourhood-r]]). The radius and coefficients may initially depend on $c$.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.
If a real power series centred at $c$ has radius $R>0$, then its sum is real analytic on $(c-R,c+R)$, interpreted as all of $\mathbb R$ when $R=+\infty$.

For $-1<x\le1$,
$$\log(1+x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}.$$
The series converges at $x=1$ to $\log2$ and diverges at $x=-1$.

On open real domains, sums and products of real-analytic functions are real analytic. If $g$ is nonzero throughout the domain, then $f/g$ is real analytic. If $g:U\to V$ and $f:V\to\mathbb R$ are real analytic, then $f\circ g$ is real analytic on $U$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim:
The finite sum gives $Z=1+e^{-\beta\epsilon}>1$, so $F$ is finite for every $\beta>0$. Differentiating with [F2] yields
$$
F'(\beta)=\frac{\log Z(\beta)}{\beta^2}+\frac{\epsilon e^{-\beta\epsilon}}{\beta Z(\beta)},
$$
whose terms are continuous on $\beta>0$.

Each derivative of $e^{-\beta\epsilon}$ is $(-\epsilon)^m e^{-\beta\epsilon}$ by induction on $m$, so $Z$ is $C^\infty$. Since $Z>0$, repeated application of the logarithm derivative formula and quotient/product rules makes every derivative of $\log Z$ continuous on $\beta>0$. The same induction gives smoothness of $\beta^{-1}$ there. Thus $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ is $C^\infty$ on $\beta>0$. To establish the stronger analytic conclusion, fix $\beta_0>0$ and $Z_0=Z(\beta_0)>0$. The exponential series and [F5] make $Z$ real analytic. On a sufficiently small neighborhood of $\beta_0$, $h(\beta):=(Z(\beta)-Z_0)/Z_0$ has $|h|<1$, and $\log Z(\beta)=\log Z_0+\log(1+h(\beta))$ by the logarithm law. The convergent log series and local analytic composition make this real analytic. The reciprocal $\beta^{-1}$ is analytic on $\beta>0$ by the nonzero-quotient clause, so $F$ is real analytic there by [F5]. Since $T\mapsto(k_BT)^{-1}$ is likewise an analytic nonzero quotient on $T>0$, the same holds in the temperature variable. Thus no nonanalytic free-energy point occurs at positive finite temperature; this says nothing about a sequence limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$. A countable probability law on $I$ means a nonnegative family with total sum $1$ under the finite-subsum convention above; these weights form such a law because $\sum_i p_i(\beta)=Z(\beta)/Z(\beta)=1$. For any real family $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials* give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of *Finite sums and finite products, by recursion*. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling*. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in *Thermodynamic response functions on valid local charts* and *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* and *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*, on the exact feasible set of *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in *Stable equilibrium requires an attained global entropy maximum*. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials* give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of *Finite sums and finite products, by recursion*. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling*. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in *Thermodynamic response functions on valid local charts* and *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* and *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*, on the exact feasible set of *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in *Stable equilibrium requires an attained global entropy maximum*. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

citations.quote:
Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

derivations.claim:
Since $0<s_0-a\le s(x)<s_0$ on $K$, every feasible $s$ is nonnegative and bounded. For $n\ge2$, put $A_n:=\{x\in K:|x|\ge1/n\}$. Each $A_n$ is Borel in $K$, the sets increase with $n$, and their union is $K$. Put $B_2=A_2$ and $B_n=A_n\setminus A_{n-1}$ for $n\ge3$. These are pairwise disjoint Borel sets with union $K$, so countable additivity gives $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}P(B_n)=P(K)=1$. Some $P(B_n)$ is therefore positive. Since $A_n=B_n\sqcup(A_n\setminus B_n)$, finite additivity and nonnegativity give $P(A_n)\ge P(B_n)>0$ for that $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n^2$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F1] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le(s_0-a/n^2)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n^2<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F1] gives the inequality. The strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$.

For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is a Borel probability measure on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon^2$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. Thus the false statement fails even with a bounded positive continuous concave extension, because the admissible generator set excludes its maximizing barycenter.

For $x\in K$, define the unit point mass $\delta_x$ by $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise, for Borel $A\subseteq K$. Assume every Borel probability mixture with barycenter $\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. Then there are $m\le d+1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in K$, and weights $\theta_i\ge0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1$ such that $P_*:=\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a feasible Borel probability mixture and $\int_Ks\,dP_*\ge\int_Ks\,dP$ for every feasible mixture $P$.

Here integrals use the measure convention of *Measure space and integral*. The entropy map is part of the model; this theorem derives neither its microscopic meaning nor compactness of a physical phase domain.

A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless generator coordinates. Each $x\in K$ labels one model-specified phase-generator state; the model assigns it entropy per mole $s(x)\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $s:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, using the numerical entropy value in that fixed unit. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ to be the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$. A Borel probability mixture is a countably additive probability measure $P$ on that sigma algebra; its barycenter and entropy per mole are the coordinatewise integrals $\int_Kx\,dP$ and $\int_Ks\,dP$. For $x\in K$, define the unit point mass $\delta_x$ by $\delta_x(A)=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise, for Borel $A\subseteq K$. Assume every Borel probability mixture with barycenter $\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks\,dP$. Then there are $m\le d+1$, points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in K$, and weights $\theta_i\ge0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1$ such that $P_*:=\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a feasible Borel probability mixture and $\int_Ks\,dP_*\ge\int_Ks\,dP$ for every feasible mixture $P$.

Here integrals use the measure convention of *Measure space and integral*. The entropy map is part of the model; this theorem derives neither its microscopic meaning nor compactness of a physical phase domain.

**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

derivations.claim: Write $w_0=P(\{0\})$ and $w_1=P(\{1\})$. By [F2], $w_0+w_1=1$ and the barycenter equation is $w_1=\tfrac12$. Hence the only feasible measure is $P_*=\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1$.

Its entropy per mole is the finite simple-function integral
$$
\int_Ks\,dP_*=\tfrac12s(0)+\tfrac12s(1)=\tfrac12s_0+\tfrac12(s_0+a)=s_0+\frac a2.
$$
Since it is the only feasible mixture, it attains the maximum. Its two support points equal $d+1$ for $d=1$, as in [F1].

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $K=\{0,1\}\subset\mathbb R$ be the compact generator domain, with dimensionless coordinate $x$. On the convex ambient domain $[0,1]$, define the affine extension $\widetilde s(x)=s_0+a x$ and restrict it to $s=\widetilde s|_K$, where fixed $s_0,a>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. For $x,y\in[0,1]$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $\widetilde s((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)\widetilde s(x)+t\widetilde s(y)$, so the extension is concave. Take the barycenter to be $\bar x=\tfrac12$ and declare every Borel probability mixture on $K$ with that barycenter feasible.

Let $d\ge1$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless phase-generator coordinates. A generator point $x\in K$ encodes one model-specified homogeneous phase state, with declared entropy per mole $s(x)$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$; let $s:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ as the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$, and let $\delta_x$ denote unit point mass at $x$. The vector integral $\int_Kx\,dP$ is taken coordinatewise. Assume every Borel probability mixture $P$ on $K$ with $\int_Kx\,dP(x)=\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks(x)\,dP(x)$. Then the entropy maximum over all such mixtures is attained by a finite atomic mixture with at most $d+1$ phase-generator states.

Here the integral uses the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map includes its physical entropy units and is part of the model; this theorem does not derive the microscopic meaning of entropy or assert that a physical phase domain is compact.

citations.quote:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. derivations.claim:
Let $\lambda_\beta:=n_\beta/N$ and $\lambda_\alpha:=n_\alpha/N$. Positivity and amount additivity give $\lambda_\alpha+\lambda_\beta=1$, with both fractions in $(0,1)$. The adopted $V_i=n_iv_i$ relation and volume additivity give
$$
\bar v:=\frac VN=\lambda_\alpha v_\alpha+\lambda_\beta v_\beta.
$$
All terms have units $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$.

Here $\bar v=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$. Solving the affine relation in step 1.1 yields
$$
\lambda_\beta=\frac{\bar v-v_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}=\frac12,\qquad \lambda_\alpha=\frac{v_\beta-\bar v}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}=\frac12.
$$
The fractions are positive and sum to one, so $n_\alpha=n_\beta=1\,\mathrm{mol}$ satisfies the given total amount and volume.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two named subsystems with disjoint physical regions as in [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], combined as a compound system $A\sqcup B$ inside a declared outer boundary. Fix their material constitutions $c_A,c_B$, each with a finite ordered list of distinct species labels as in [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Fix an ordering $(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)$ of the labels occurring in either list, each occurring once, and use this as the species list of the compound constitution $c_{A\sqcup B}$. For $s\in\{A,B,A\sqcup B\}$, write $D_s:=D_{c_s}$ and use $U_s,V_s$ for its dimensioned coordinate maps. For every $1\le j\le r$, define the aligned amount map $a_{s,j}:D_s\to[0,\infty)\,\mathrm{mol}$ by $a_{s,j}(x):=n_{c_s,k}(x)$ if $\sigma_j$ is the $k$-th species in $c_s$'s list, and $a_{s,j}(x):=0\,\mathrm{mol}$ if it is absent. Distinctness makes $k$ unique. The absent-species value is a bookkeeping map on the existing $D_s$; it does not insert a zero coordinate into that constitution's positive-mole chart or assert a boundary-state extension.

The model's admitted separated pairs form a specified subset $\mathcal C_{AB}\subseteq D_A\times D_B$ using [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]] and [[def-cartesian-product]]. Adopt a composition function $\kappa_{AB}:\mathcal C_{AB}\to D_{A\sqcup B}$ ([[def-function]]) such that, for every $(x_A,x_B)\in\mathcal C_{AB}$ and every $1\le j\le r$, its output satisfies
$$U_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=U_A(x_A)+U_B(x_B),\qquad V_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=V_A(x_A)+V_B(x_B),\qquad a_{A\sqcup B,j}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=a_{A,j}(x_A)+a_{B,j}(x_B).$$
All quantities have the SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. Each union species is present in at least one constituent with positive amount, so the summed amount is positive and agrees with the compound's $j$-th coordinate. The existence of an output in the declared $D_{A\sqcup B}$ is part of the adopted model, not a consequence of positivity.

Here “extensive coordinates” means precisely the named coordinates declared additive by this postulate. This is an idealized composition rule: cross-interface and long-range interaction energy is omitted from $U_{A\sqcup B}$, rather than asserted to vanish in nature. The postulate does not assert that every pair of subsystem states is physically admissible.

The framework's bulk family is a tagged family of material types. For each dimensionless scale $\lambda>0$ the model may designate a tag $c^{(\lambda)}$ with the same ordered species list and SI coordinate conventions as $c$, and a subset $B_{c,\lambda}\subseteq D_c$ of states admitting a scaled copy, with inclusion as in [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in B_{c,\lambda}$, the scaling map is the function $\delta_\lambda:B_{c,\lambda}\to D_{c^{(\lambda)}}$ ([[def-function]]) given by $\delta_\lambda(x)=(\lambda\hat U,\lambda\hat V,\lambda\hat n_1,\ldots,\lambda\hat n_r)$. The tag matters: $c^{(\lambda)}$ is not silently identified with $c$. This postulate specifies the coordinate scaling model and energy additivity only; it does not postulate entropy additivity or exact scaling for every finite physical body.

This is an adopted physical composition rule, not a deduction from SI units or from the mathematics of Cartesian products.

citations.quote:
Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from *Phase branches and coexistence domains* on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of *Euler and Gibbs-Duhem identities under same-tag homogeneity* when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by *SI quantities and unit conventions*. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, and the full finite isolated compound (converted phases, reservoir, work stores and all auxiliaries) has equilibrium endpoints with additive component entropy, with every component other than the converted phases and that reservoir having zero entropy change, and the admitted forward and reverse complete-compound records have nonnegative total endpoint entropy changes for that same additive split with their full endpoint tuples interchanged, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. These are conditional model deductions. The slope conclusion is not asserted when $\Delta v=0$ or where the branch charts are not $C^1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim:
At $(T_0,p_0)$, differentiation gives $S_i/n_i=s_i$, $V_i/n_i=v_0$, and $\mu_i=g_i=g_0$. Also $U_{i,T}=n_i c$, $V_{i,p}=-n_i\kappa$, and $V_{i,T}=0$, so the derivative determinant for $(T,p)\mapsto(U_i,V_i)$ at fixed positive amount is $-n_i^2c\kappa\ne0$. Thus [L1] supplies valid local state charts. The branch equality function is
$$
F(T,p):=g_\beta-g_\alpha=-(s_\beta-s_\alpha)(T-T_0),
$$
whose zero set is $T=T_0$ with every nearby chart pressure permitted.

Here $\Delta v=v_\beta-v_\alpha=0$, so the zero set is not the graph of a unique pressure as a function of temperature on an open interval about $T_0$, and the quotient $\Delta s/\Delta v$ is undefined. The nonzero-jump hypothesis of [F1] fails, so this model does not contradict that theorem.

Fix $T_0>0$, $p_0>0$, $g_0\in\mathbb R$, $v_0,c,\kappa>0$, and distinct positive molar entropies $s_\alpha,s_\beta$. Use units $g_0\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $v_0\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, $c\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\kappa\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. On a common open chart define
$$
g_i(T,p)=g_0-s_i(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_0(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,
$$
with $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$. Let $G_i=n_i g_i$ and adopt $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$, and $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$. This gives same-tag scaling and smooth local Gibbs charts. At $(T_0,p_0)$ the molar Gibbs values agree and the molar-volume jump is zero; the entropies differ.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials* give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of *Finite sums and finite products, by recursion*. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling*. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in *Thermodynamic response functions on valid local charts* and *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

The branch theorems on this page require the stated smooth local charts. Here coexistence means equality of the declared intensive phase data at an admitted endpoint; it does not itself imply loss of chart regularity. The smooth-branch conclusions apply only on their specified C1 charts and interior composition domains. They supply no conclusion where a branch chart fails to be C1, a species amount reaches the composition boundary, or the specified coexistence-and-affinity Jacobian lacks its required nonsingular minor. In particular, [[pthm-td-clapeyron-local]] requires a nonzero molar-volume jump; when that jump vanishes, its local graph argument and quotient formula do not apply.

The compact-mixture result [[pthm-td-compact-continuous-phase-mixture]] requires a compact phase-generator domain, a continuous entropy map, a fixed barycenter, and feasibility of all probability mixtures with that barycenter. It supplies no attainment theorem for noncompact domains. Likewise, [[def-td-thermodynamic-limit-contract]] specifies the sequence and normalization for a limiting claim but proves no limit exists and no derivatives commute with that limit.

A finite-state partition sum is finite and positive at each finite system size. A singular phase behavior therefore needs a separately specified limit or another model with a separately established domain and regularity analysis. This page does not assert a universal thermodynamic-limit theorem, ensemble equivalence, critical exponent, or physical applicability of the van der Waals equation.

The local homogeneity used by [[pthm-td-clapeyron-local]] may be independently stipulated in a phase model or supplied on the separately designated common-law bulk branch under the local Euler theorem's inverse-chart and common-reference conditions. A constructed local Gibbs model need not be embedded in a global bulk cone to use the general conditional result. The added branch supplies no universal finite-size, long-range or gravitational extensivity and does not remove any smoothness, exchange or nonzero-volume-jump condition.
